title: If you can damage, you can repair
hookLine: Rebbe Nachman: if you believe you can damage, believe you can repair
carry: teshuvah: if you can damage, you can repair
last: JOY IS A MITZVAH, KEPT UP ON HARD DAYS.

lines: THE LIST STARTS TO FEEL LIKE PROOF.
cards: "I ruin everything." Some people say it out loud after a bad day. Some only think it.

A sharp word at dinner, a forgotten promise, a friendship that went quiet because you didn't call. The list gets long, and it starts to feel like proof. Here's something odd about that sentence, though.
It takes your power very seriously. It believes, completely, that what you do has effects. Rebbe Nachman of Breslov noticed exactly that, and turned it around.

teach.h: THE SAME HANDS, THE SAME POWER.
teach.b: You can repair. Rebbe Nachman taught, in words his students wrote down: if you believe that you can damage, then believe that you can repair. First, the logic.
It's almost a trick of fairness. You already believe your actions matter, because you believe they did harm. Fine, he says.
Then you can't turn around and claim your actions are powerless when it comes to fixing. The same hands. The same power.
Second, the old root. This isn't new to Hasidism.
The prophet Ezekiel tells the people to cast away their wrongs and "make you a new heart and a new spirit." Make. As if a heart is something a person can work on.
That's the heart of teshuvah, returning: the door is open, and you can walk through it.
Third, the enemy. For Rebbe Nachman, the great danger after a wrong isn't the wrong itself. It's despair, the conclusion that nothing can be done.
Breslov teaching treasures his saying that there is no despair in the world at all. Despair closes the door teshuvah opens. Fourth, the scale.

Repair doesn't have to be large. Brought home, the teaching works at the size of an apology, a phone call, a mended chair, a sentence you take back. His teaching doesn't ask for everything to be repaired.
It asks for one repair, seen as possible, and then made.

how: In Jewish practice teshuvah, returning, means admitting a wrong, regretting it, making it right with anyone harmed, and resolving to change; Breslov teaching stresses never giving up on that return.

o: a promise that past wrongs are erased by themselves
the power that can harm can also mend
a rule that every broken thing must be replaced

games.q: you've broken something, a promise, a friendship. a voice says: I ruin everything. what's Rebbe Nachman's answer?
o: if you believe you can damage, believe you can repair.
games.why: he turns the belief around: the same power that did harm can mend. despair is the real danger.

practice: Let one small damage come to mind, something you broke or let slide that you could actually touch today, and look at it without the old sentence, I ruin everything.
Instead, say Rebbe Nachman's turn to yourself, if I could damage it, I can repair it, and picture the first step: the text, the fix, the words. If you pray, you can ask for help with the step.

wordCard.voice: You can repair. Rebbe Nachman's teaching: if you believe you can damage, believe you can repair. The same power that harms can mend. Today's words.

orig.note: Hebrew: to repair, to set right. The verb behind tikkun, repair.
